sources.title: Human History Map historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository entry checked: emirate-of-tiflis is labeled Emirate of Tiflis, marked circa and historical-basemaps generated, and indexed 1100 to 1200 without aliases or an authored link.

sources.title: Human History Map imported historical-basemap summaries
sources.note: Imported summary checked for its Wikipedia provenance and its internally important distinction between effective emir rule to about 1080 and Georgian capture of the city in 1122.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1000 topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor seam. The target id is absent and the imported Georgia feature owns all audited eastern Georgian city tests, including the exact modern Tbilisi point.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1100 topology
sources.note: Decoded only target layer. It contains one unlabeled seven-position Polygon southeast of Tbilisi; exact Tbilisi and every named audit point miss it, while Georgia owns the city point.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1200 topology
sources.note: Decoded endpoint seam. The exact target disappears and the Georgia feature owns Tbilisi, Mtskheta, Rustavi, Gori, Dmanisi, Telavi and Kutaisi at the 1200 snapshot.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1279 topology
sources.note: Decoded later successor seam. The target remains absent; Ilkhanate geometry overlays several eastern Georgian and Caucasian tests while Georgia retains Gori and Kutaisi.

sources.title: Emirate of Tbilisi, Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Georgian National Academy of Sciences encyclopedia entry checked for establishment, caliphal administration, territorial contraction, Shuabids, Jaffarids, coinage, Georgian pressure and rule by city elders after the 1080s.

sources.title: Bugha al-Kabir's Campaign, Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Academy encyclopedia entry checked for the 853 to 854 campaign, Ishaq's rebellion, participating alliances, the crossing into Tbilisi, destruction, execution and the chroniclers' casualty claims.

sources.title: Tbilisi Fortress (Narikala), Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Academy encyclopedia entry checked for the citadel's changing names, early fortifications, Bagrat IV's 1045 seizure and David IV's securing of fortress and city in 1122.

sources.title: Tbileli Berebi (Elders of Tbilisi), Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Georgian-language Academy entry checked for elite citizen representation, opposition to emirs, full urban government from the Jaffarids' extinction in the 1080s to 1122 and al-Fariqi's rotating-rule report.

sources.title: Abo Tbileli, Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Academy encyclopedia biography checked for Abo's approximate dates, Arab background, service to Nerse, skill mixing myrrh preparations, conversion, execution and contemporary Georgian hagiography.

sources.title: al-Tiflisi, Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Georgian-language Academy entry checked for the nisba's meaning and for connected theologians, jurists, writers, poets, physicians, merchants and craftspeople, including al-Hasan and Hubaysh.

sources.title: Tiflis, TDV Encyclopedia of Islam
sources.note: Scholarly encyclopedia entry checked for geography, the seventh-century agreement, emirate politics, Bagratid and Seljuk episodes, fortifications, baths, mixed worship, products, crafts and David IV's capture.

sources.title: The Seventh Century Conquest of Kartli by Habib ibn Maslamah
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Tbilisi State University article checked for the 654 to 655 peace-and-security agreement, its household rather than individual levy and scholarly cautions about transmitted treaty texts.

sources.title: Abbasid dirhems of Tbilisi mint, Online English-Georgian Catalogue of Georgian Numismatics
sources.note: Tbilisi State University numismatic catalogue checked for the AH 248 / 862 to 63 issue, known specimens, metal and dimensions, and the complete original Arabic legends with translation.

sources.title: Jaffarid dirhems of Tbilisi mint, Online English-Georgian Catalogue of Georgian Numismatics
sources.note: Tbilisi State University catalogue checked for the Jaffarid dynasty, rulers revealed by coins, issues of AH 342 to 418 and what names and dates show about hereditary local power.

sources.title: The History of Emirs of Tbilisi According to Numismatic Materials
sources.note: Institute of Georgian History study checked for reconstructed Jaffarid successions, otherwise unknown rulers, debased late issues, hoards and the evidence and limits of coins as political sources.

sources.title: A new dirham of Ja'far ibn Mansur struck at Tiflis
sources.note: Oriental Numismatic Society article checked for identification of a Tiflis issue of AH 374 / 984 to 85 and the way one coin adds to the fragmentary record of hereditary emirs.

sources.title: Researches into the History of Georgia and the Near East
sources.note: National Parliamentary Library volume checked for the al-Tiflisi biographical corpus, its explicit evidence limits, occupations, education journeys, religious currents and post-1122 Muslim continuity.

sources.title: Banu Saj, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly reference checked for Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj's Caucasian campaigns, occupation of Tiflis after conflict with Smbat and the wider politics of Azerbaijan, Armenia and caliphal investiture around 900.

sources.title: Caucasica in the History of Mayyafariqin
sources.note: Minorsky's source study checked for al-Fariqi's Caucasian material, the elders' invitation to Ilghazi, the 1122 capture and cautions when reconciling Georgian and Arabic chronologies.

sources.title: Tbilisi (Georgia), UNESCO World Heritage documentation
sources.note: UNESCO dossier checked for Tbilisi's fortified urban development, trading and administrative roles, early medieval churches, the 853 destruction, revival and incorporation into David IV's kingdom.

sources.title: Islamic-Arabic Sources on Medieval Tbilisi, Pro Georgia 30
sources.note: Scholarly source survey checked for al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal and al-Muqaddasi on walls, gates, river, fertile surroundings, crops, fruit, thermal water and the limits of translating geographic descriptions.

sources.title: Tbilisi Mosques in Georgian and Foreign Sources
sources.note: Turkish Historical Society congress study checked for mosque institutions, khatib and qadi, wooden urban fabric, Muslim worship before and after 1122 and the survival limits of early structures.

sources.title: Georgia and the Near Eastern Islamic World in the Twelfth to Early Thirteenth Century
sources.note: National Parliamentary Library study checked for privileges granted after 1122, continued worship and qadi jurisdiction, Arabic-inscribed coinage and the careful analogy with protected communities.

sources.title: Challenges in Urban Archaeology in Tbilisi
sources.note: Recent archaeological report checked for medieval ceramic production, kilns, vessels, cellars, water reservoirs and tubes, refuse practices, dating problems and the preliminary character of many interpretations.

sources.title: One Aspect of the Tbilisi Water Supply System in the 19th Century
sources.note: Art-academy journal article checked for river, well and ceramic-pipe supply traditions and its explicit warning that exposed pipe dates and supposed medieval continuity remain uncertain without excavation.

sources.title: Glazed Clay Pottery in Eastern Georgia of the Middle Ages
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeology article checked for ninth to thirteenth-century local bowls and dishes, red and kaolin clays, glazing and painted motifs, including material from a medieval Tbilisi workshop.

sources.title: Archaeology of the Dmanisi Medieval Town
sources.note: Municipal archaeological overview checked for the emirate-linked regional city's houses, workshops, glass and pottery production, fortifications, bath, water-supply tunnel and later rebuilding chronology.

sources.title: Dmanisi medieval necropolis, new epigraphic evidence
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Georgian National Museum-led study checked for Dmanisi's ninth-century urban role, trade routes and multi-confessional Georgian, Armenian and Arabic epigraphic record.

sources.title: Education in Medieval Georgia (11th to 12th Centuries)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed education-history article checked for household, religious and formal learning distinctions, church and monastery centers, travel for advanced study and the rise of Georgian academies around the conquest era.

sources.title: Isa al-Raqqi al-Tiflisi in A Literary History of Medicine
sources.note: Critical edition hosted by NCBI Bookshelf checked for the tenth-century al-Tiflisi physician-translator at Sayf al-Dawla's court and for what the biographical anecdote does and does not show about Tbilisi.

sources.title: Comparative analysis of medieval Georgian and European medical treatises and remedies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed history-of-science article checked for the eleventh-century Georgian Ustsoro Karabadini, remedies, wine and classical knowledge, used only as regional written medicine rather than proof of an emirate clinic.

sources.title: Hubaysh al-Tiflisi, Islamisation of Anatolia prosopography
sources.note: Research-project record checked for the Tiflis-born physician, astronomer and author, his migration, Arabic and Persian works and the uncertainty in his death date.

sources.title: Ioane Sabanisdze, The Martyrdom of Abo Tbileli
sources.note: Tbilisi State University-hosted edition of the eighth-century Georgian hagiography checked as near-contemporary evidence for language learning, craft skill, religious conflict and the source's devotional genre.

sources.title: Early Arabic inscriptions and administration in Tiflis, Chronos 3
sources.note: Scholarly journal study checked for the Kufic inscription dated Sha'ban AH 147, early Tiflis minting and the administrative significance of Arabic writing in the eighth-century city.

sources.title: Social and Legal Status of Women in Medieval Georgia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed regional legal-history study checked for ninth-century evidence of dowry and women's property interests; used with an explicit warning that broad Georgian evidence cannot fill Tbilisi-specific silence.

sources.title: Battle of Didgori, Georgian Encyclopedia
sources.note: Georgian National Academy of Sciences encyclopedia entry checked for the 1121 coalition, Tbilisi's strategic relation to Didgori and David IV's victory, without repeating disputed giant army totals.

proposedOverrides.summary: A Muslim-ruled Caucasian crossroads became a self-governing city by the 1080s and Georgia's capital after 1122, despite an atlas shape lingering to 1200.

fell.text: David IV captured Tbilisi and its citadel in 1122, ending the city elders' independent government and incorporating the city into the Kingdom of Georgia.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target emirate-of-tiflis is indexed circa 1100 to 1200, has no alias or authored link, and had no tracked card or researched override before isolated integration.

The only target geometry is an unlabeled seven-position Polygon in world-1100; its bounds lie southeast of Tbilisi, and its coordinate-array SHA-256 is 0b1e8ea8b03040ea69734d51090a11e799fe1fc89177811132b93263f53c24b1.

Exact modern Tbilisi and every other named audit point miss the target polygon. The separate Georgia feature owns Tbilisi, and the target shares raw topology arcs only with Georgia and Kakheti-Hereti.
The target is absent at 1000, 1200 and 1279. This is an imported locator and seam artifact rather than a historically faithful boundary series.

Historical phases are separated: treaty and tribute around 654 to 655; caliphal emirate from the 730s; Shuabid and Jaffarid local power; city elders after the 1080s; Georgian conquest in 1122; post-conquest continuity through the atlas cutoff.
The historical date problem is explicit: effective emir rule ended around 1080, independent civic rule ended in 1122, and the atlas label persists to 1200.
Daily-life claims separate Tbilisi evidence from regional comparisons and later continuity. No standard household, school attendance rate, outfit, menu, cure, game, toilet or sewer is invented.
The written sample is a formal Arabic mint legend struck at Tbilisi in AH 248 / 862 to 63, with original script, transliteration, translation, date and genre; it is not labeled as ordinary speech.
No appliesTo alias or shared-card substitution is used.
